key_terms.meaning: Value of a state variable just before switching, at t = 0⁻, written i_L(0⁻) or v_C(0⁻).
Inductor current and capacitor voltage cannot jump: i_L(0⁺) = i_L(0⁻) and v_C(0⁺) = v_C(0⁻).
Steady value at t → ∞ found with L replaced by a short and C by an open for DC sources.
τ = L/R for an RL circuit, τ = RC for an RC circuit; the time in which the change reaches 63.2% of its final value.
A circuit with no independent source after t = 0, so only stored energy drives the response.
The part of the answer produced by the circuit's own stored energy and roots; it decays with time in a passive circuit.
The part of the answer fixed by the source alone; for a constant or sine source it equals the steady-state response.
Natural part plus forced part, conveniently written x(t) = x(∞) + [x(0⁺) − x(∞)]e^(−t/τ) for a first-order circuit.
The equation that gives the natural roots; for a series RLC it is s² + (R/L)s + 1/(LC) = 0.
Overdamped = two distinct real roots, critically damped = equal real roots, underdamped = complex roots.
α = R/(2L) for a series RLC and α = 1/(2RC) for a parallel RLC, measured in rad/s (also called nepers per second).
ω_n = 1/√(LC) rad/s; the frequency the circuit would ring at if resistance were zero.
ζ = α/ω_n, dimensionless; for a series RLC, ζ = (R/2)√(C/L).
ω_d = ω_n√(1 − ζ²) rad/s, the actual ringing frequency when ζ < 1.
F(s) = ∫₀^∞ f(t)e^(−st)dt, with s = σ + jω, the complex frequency.
Inductance L becomes impedance sL with a series source L i_L(0⁻); capacitance C becomes 1/(sC) with a series source v_C(0⁻)/s.
H(s) = Y(s)/X(s) with all independent sources killed and zero initial energy.
Poles are roots of the denominator of H(s) and give the natural response; zeros are roots of the numerator and shape the forced response.
x = [i_L, v_C]ᵀ, the set of energy variables that completely describes the circuit at any instant.
f(0⁺) = lim s→∞ sF(s), a quick check on an inverse Laplace answer.

takeaways: Inductor current and capacitor voltage are the two quantities that cannot jump, so the circuit state at t = 0⁻ decides the whole answer after switching.
With no source, energy drains as a pure exponential e^(−t/τ) whose speed is fixed only by R and the storage element.
Every first-order answer is final value plus (initial value minus final value) times e^(−t/τ); find the two end values and τ and the work is done.
Two storage elements give a quadratic characteristic equation, and its two roots decide whether the answer creeps, settles cleanly, or rings.
The pair ω_n and ζ replaces R, L and C as the description of a second-order circuit: ω_n sets how fast it wants to oscillate, ζ sets how fast the oscillation is killed.
With a sine source the complete response is a steady-state sine plus a decaying exponential whose size depends on the instant of switching.
The Laplace transform turns the differential equation into algebra and puts the initial conditions inside the circuit as extra sources.
With sources killed and zero initial energy the circuit is a single ratio H(s); its poles give the natural response and its zeros shape the steady-state response.
State variables turn any circuit into ẋ = Ax + Bu and y = Cx + Du, where the eigenvalues of A are the natural frequencies.
bank_note: Long answers are expected to combine a derivation with a worked numerical example, and to justify initial and final conditions from continuity before writing the solution.

bank.q: State and explain the continuity conditions for an inductor and a capacitor. Why can these two quantities not change instantaneously, while resistor current and voltage can?
outline: Inductor: v_L = L di/dt, so a jump in i would need infinite voltage — not possible in a physical circuit.
Capacitor: i_C = C dv/dt, so a jump in v would need infinite current.
Hence i_L(0⁺) = i_L(0⁻) and v_C(0⁺) = v_C(0⁻).
Resistor obeys v = iR with no memory, so it may jump freely.
Stored energy ½Li² and ½Cv² cannot change in zero time.

bank.q: Define the time constant of an RC circuit and of an RL circuit. Give its unit, and state the meaning of one, three and five time constants.
outline: τ = RC seconds; τ = L/R seconds.
Unit: seconds when R in ohms, C in farads, L in henries.
One τ: change reaches 63.2% of final value (rises to 36.8% of initial gap remaining).
Three τ: about 95%; five τ: about 99.3%, treated as steady state.
Sketch of the exponential and the tangent at t = 0 cutting the final value at t = τ.

bank.q: Distinguish between natural response, forced response and complete response of a linear circuit. Show how the three are added for a first-order circuit with a DC source.
outline: Natural: source set to zero, set by circuit roots, always decays in a passive circuit.
Forced: source kept, found as the steady state; constant for DC input.
Complete = natural + forced.
Working form x(t) = x(∞) + [x(0⁺) − x(∞)]e^(−t/τ).
Verify by checking t = 0⁺ and t → ∞.

bank.q: Explain how the roots of the characteristic equation of a series RLC circuit classify the response as overdamped, critically damped or underdamped. State the condition on R in each case.
outline: Characteristic equation s² + (R/L)s + 1/(LC) = 0.
Roots s₁,₂ = −α ± √(α² − ω_n²) with α = R/(2L), ω_n = 1/√(LC).
α > ω_n i.e. R > 2√(L/C): overdamped, two real roots.
α = ω_n i.e. R = 2√(L/C): critically damped, repeated root.
α < ω_n i.e. R < 2√(L/C): underdamped, complex conjugate roots, response rings.
Sketch the three waveforms.

bank.q: A 100 V DC source charges a 20 μF capacitor through a 50 kΩ resistor. The switch is opened at t = 0 after steady state. Find v_C(t), the time constant, and the time for the capacitor to fall to 20 V.
outline: v_C(0⁻) = 100 V, continuity gives v_C(0⁺) = 100 V.
v_C(t) = 100e^(−t) V for t ≥ 0.
Note the discharge path and that i_C is negative.

bank.q: In an RL circuit, a 10 Ω resistor and a 2 H inductor are suddenly connected to a 20 V battery at t = 0, with i_L(0⁻) = 0. Find i_L(t), the voltage across the inductor, and the energy stored at t = 1 s.
outline: v_L = L di/dt = 20e^(−5t) V, check t = 0⁺ gives 20 V and t → ∞ gives 0 V.

bank.q: A series RLC circuit has R = 5 Ω, L = 1 H and C = 0.25 F, and is switched on to a 10 V DC source at t = 0 with zero initial energy. Find α, ω_n, ζ, classify the response, and write the complete expression for i(t).
outline: ω_n = 1/√(LC) = 2 rad/s.
ζ = α/ω_n = 1.25 > 1 → overdamped.
i(0⁺) = 0 and di/dt(0⁺) = V/L = 10, giving i(t) = A₁e^(−t) + A₂e^(−4t).

bank.q: An RL circuit with R = 4 Ω and L = 1 H is connected at t = 0 to v(t) = 20 sin(100t + 30°) V. Find the complete current response and identify the transient and steady-state parts.
outline: Steady state by phasors: Z = 4 + j100, |Z| ≈ 100.08, angle ≈ 87.7°.
Transient term Ke^(−4t), τ = 0.25 s.
Use i(0⁺) = i(0⁻) = 0 to find K.
Complete i(t) = i_ss(t) + Ke^(−4t); state that the transient dies in about 5τ.

bank.q: Use the Laplace transform to solve for v_C(t) in a series RC circuit with R = 2 Ω, C = 0.5 F, v_C(0⁻) = 5 V, switched at t = 0 to a 10 V source. Verify your answer with the initial and final value theorems.
outline: s-domain: (10/s) = I(s)R + I(s)/(sC) + v_C(0⁻)/s.
Solve for V_C(s) = 10/s − 2I(s) or use node equation directly.
τ = RC = 1 s, so v_C(t) = 10 − 5e^(−t) V.
Initial value theorem: lim s→∞ sV_C(s) = 5 V = v_C(0⁺).
Final value theorem: lim s→0 sV_C(s) = 10 V = v_C(∞).
Correct partial fraction step shown.

bank.q: For a series RLC circuit with L = 1 H and C = 1 F, find the value of R that gives critical damping. Plot the shape of the capacitor voltage for R above and below this value, and explain the physical reason for the difference.
outline: Critical damping when R = 2√(L/C) = 2 Ω.
α = R/(2L), ω_n = 1 rad/s, ζ = R/2.
R > 2 Ω: overdamped, slow creep to final value, no overshoot.
R < 2 Ω: underdamped, ringing at ω_d = √(1 − ζ²), overshoot above final value.
Physical reason: larger R dissipates the stored energy faster than it can be exchanged between L and C.
Comment on the envelope e^(−αt) and on settling time.

bank.q: A sinusoidal source is switched onto an RL circuit. Show that the size of the transient term depends on the switching angle, and find the switching instant at which the transient is zero.
outline: i(t) = I_m sin(ωt + θ − φ) + Ke^(−t/τ), with φ = tan⁻¹(ωL/R).
i(0⁺) = 0 fixes K = −I_m sin(θ − φ).
K = 0 when θ = φ, i.e. switching at the instant the steady-state current is passing through zero going positive.
Worst case is θ − φ = ±90°, where the transient has peak amplitude I_m.
Practical comment: this is why inrush current in transformers and motors depends on the instant of switching.

bank.q: For the circuit with a series RLC branch, write the state equations in the form ẋ = Ax + Bu, identify the state variables, and show how the eigenvalues of A relate to the natural response.
outline: Choose x₁ = i_L, x₂ = v_C.
L dx₁/dt = −Rx₁ − x₂ + u; C dx₂/dt = x₁.
Eigenvalues from det(sI − A) = 0, which reproduces s² + (R/L)s + 1/(LC) = 0.
Output equation y = Cx + Du for the chosen output.
State that eigenvalues of A are the natural frequencies.

bank.q: Define the transfer function of a network. For a given two-port network, explain how the pole-zero plot predicts stability and the shape of the impulse response.
outline: H(s) = Y(s)/X(s) with sources killed and zero initial energy.
Poles are roots of the denominator, zeros of the numerator.
All poles in the left half plane → stable; poles on the jω axis → marginal; right half plane → unstable.
Real pole gives e^(−σt); complex pair gives e^(−σt)cos(ω_d t + φ).
Zero near the jω axis reduces the response at that frequency, i.e. it notches the steady-state gain.
Impulse response is the inverse Laplace transform of H(s).

bank.q: A circuit with one capacitor and one inductor is switched at t = 0. Outline the full method for finding any branch voltage using the Laplace transform, stating where the initial conditions enter and how the answer is checked.
outline: Find v_C(0⁻) and i_L(0⁻) in the t < 0 circuit with L short and C open.
Apply continuity to get 0⁺ values.
Draw the s-domain circuit: sL with series source L i_L(0⁻), 1/(sC) with series source v_C(0⁻)/s.
Write mesh or nodal equations and solve for the wanted transform.
Inverse transform by partial fractions.
Check with initial and final value theorems and with physical reasoning about 0⁺ and ∞.

glossary.def: The part of a response that dies away with time after a change in the circuit.
The condition reached after the transient has vanished, when every quantity repeats or stays constant.
An abrupt change in the circuit at t = 0, usually by closing or opening a switch.
A fall of the form Ae^(−t/τ), in which equal time steps give equal fractional drops.
The value τ in e^(−t/τ); the time for the response to fall to 36.8% of its starting value.
The response of a circuit after its source is removed, driven only by stored energy.
The response produced by the circuit's own poles with independent sources set to zero.
The response forced by the source, equal to the steady state for DC and sine inputs.
The polynomial equation whose roots are the natural frequencies of the circuit.
A value of s that makes the natural response possible; written s₁ and s₂ for a second-order circuit.
The loss of oscillatory energy caused by resistance, which makes a second-order response settle.
A second-order case with two distinct real roots; the response settles without oscillating.
The boundary case with equal real roots; the fastest settling without overshoot.
A second-order case with complex roots; the response oscillates while it decays.
The dimensionless number α/ω_n that measures how strongly oscillation is suppressed.
The frequency in rad/s at which the circuit would oscillate with no resistance.
The actual oscillation frequency ω_n√(1 − ζ²) when the circuit is underdamped.
A rule that maps a time function f(t) to a complex-frequency function F(s).
The step that recovers f(t) from F(s), usually by partial fractions and a table.
Splitting a ratio of polynomials into simple terms whose inverse transforms are known.
The ratio Y(s)/X(s) of output to input transform for zero initial energy.
A value of s where the transfer function becomes infinite and the natural response lives.
A value of s where the transfer function becomes zero, blocking transmission at that frequency.
The output when the input is a unit impulse; it is the inverse Laplace transform of H(s).
The complex plane with σ on the horizontal axis and jω on the vertical axis, used to plot poles and zeros.
One of the minimum set of quantities, here i_L and v_C, that fixes the future behaviour of the circuit.
